To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
obese patients lose 3 litres of water per kilogram of weight lost during the initial phase of dieting and retain 2.3 litres per kilogram during the later phase of weight loss.
the initial water loss of obese patients on dieting is due mainly to a loss of body sodium and that the subsequent water retention is due to a retention of body sodium.
obese patients who are losing weight on a reducing regimen are in a state of negative sodium balance and positive potassium balance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the water and electrolyte exchanges in obese patients who are attempting to reduce their weight.

(a) the water and electrolyte exchanges which take place during the course of a reducing regimen; (b) the relationship between these changes and the metabolic rate, the body water content and the weight of the patients; and (c) the changes in the body composition of the patients during this period of weight loss.

the changes in the total water and electrolyte balances of obese patients during weight reduction, and in particular with the changes in sodium and potassium balances which are associated with the water balance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the water and electrolyte balance studies on the obese patients showed that the water and the electrolyte losses during the first week of the treatment were much greater than the subsequent losses.
the water and electrolyte exchanges during the first week of treatment are consistent with the view that the obese carry a relative water overload which they rapidly lose by dehydration.
obese patients on a strict reducing diet lose water rapidly at first, but thereafter they retain water, and that this retention is associated with an increase in their sodium and potassium balance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
obese people who lose weight by dieting lose more water in the first week of treatment than is subsequently retained.
obese subjects, when placed on a strict reducing regimen, show an initial water loss of 1-3 litres, which is followed by a secondary water retention of 0-6-0-8 litre.
the water and electrolyte balance studies of obese patients on strict reducing diets showed a marked tendency towards a positive water and sodium balance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
obese patients on a strict reducing regimen may retain water and sodium in excess of their intake, even in the absence of edema.
obese patients on a strict reducing diet have a high water intake and excrete large volumes of urine and faecally derived water, but the water content of the diet is increased.
obese people who are losing weight by dieting have a tendency to retain water, and that this is due to a sodium retention.
